title: Storage Meter Pressure Lab
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Learning Analytics
LRS-Lite
Browser Storage
IndexedDB
description: Set the size, backup age and unsynced age of an LRS-Lite browser database, predict which pressure level (Normal, Offer, Reclaim or Protect) the storage meter triggers, then see which slices the library discards first.
audience: Teachers, instructional designers, learning-technology developers and learning-analytics practitioners (college undergraduate and professional development)

educational.topic: The LRS-Lite 10 MB budget, storage meter and pressure levels
learningObjectives: The learner will predict which pressure level a given storage state triggers and which data the library discards first.
prerequisites: IndexedDB storage and its object stores (Chapter 22)
The 10 MB budget and its slices (Chapter 22)

accessibility.notes: All controls are native p5 DOM elements; describe() is updated with the current state and, after a prediction, the level. Slice tooltips need a pointer; the legend repeats every slice size as text.

controls.label: Keep my record on this device

keyQuestions: Which level does this state trigger, and which rule decides it?
What does the library discard first?
Why does Protect need unsynced data?
commonMisconceptions: That summaries can be pruned to save space
That granted persistence changes the budget or level
assessmentOpportunities: Write the discard order from memory

simulation.modelType: rule-based state model with prediction gate
equations: Protect if pct >= 95 and unsynced hours > 0
Offer if pct >= 60 or days >= 7 or hours > 24
Normal otherwise; the highest matching level wins
illustrative slices: summaries = min(1, 0.25 S), unsealed = min(0.5, 0.05 S), mirrored = 0.2 S, device = rest
assumptions: Growth per 10 days uses the design heavy-student figures (0.37 MB and 3.6 MB per 90-day semester)
Reclaim frees space down to just under 80%; at Protect the Reclaim drops also apply
0 h of unsynced age means nothing is waiting
limitations: The meter and levels are a design, not built code
Slice split and covered-segment amounts are illustrative
